421.title: Before I formed thee (Jeremiah 1)
421.hook: a young man says I am a child, and God says I knew thee before
421.howItsDone: Catholics hear Jeremiah's call at Mass, and the Catechism cites Jeremiah 1:5 in its teaching on the dignity of human life from conception.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the suffering servant, the man of sorrows whose wounds heal others. Your line was by his bruises. Whose burden did you lighten? Day four hundred twenty-one, and a new week, and a new prophet.

He comes from a family of priests in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The book tells us when: the thirteenth year of King Josiah, and on until Jerusalem is carried away captive. He's young. How young, we don't know; the text only lets him call himself a boy. And he's about to be handed a hard job: to tell his own people, year after year, that disaster is coming, and to watch them ignore him, and then to watch it happen. His name is Jeremiah, Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims. And it begins with God telling him something about before he was born.
screen: `A PRIEST'S SON FROM ANATHOTH.` → `THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF JOSIAH.` → `A HARD JOB.`

segments.voice: The word of the Lord comes to him, and in the Douay-Rheims it says: "Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee: and before thou camest forth out of the womb, I sanctified thee, and made thee a prophet unto the nations." Notice the order. Known first. Then set apart. Then given a job. Before Jeremiah did anything, before he was anything, he was known. And Jeremiah's answer is honest. In the Douay: "Ah, ah, ah, Lord God: behold, I cannot speak, for I am a child." Ah, ah, ah. Stammering. God doesn't argue about his age. He says: say not, I am a child. You'll go where I send you. Be not afraid, for I am with thee. Then God touches his mouth, the way the coal touched Isaiah's lips: I have given my words in thy mouth. Then a strange little test. What do you see, Jeremiah? A branch of an almond tree. Good, God says, for I am watching over my word. In Hebrew it's a pun: almond is shaqed, watching is shoqed. Some readers explain the name: the almond wakes early in spring, the watchful tree. The Douay, following the Latin, simply calls it a rod watching. The Catholic Church has taken that first line further than Jeremiah's own story. The Catechism quotes it in its teaching that human life is to be respected and protected from the moment of conception. For Jeremiah, that knowing came first, before all the hard years.
screen: `KNOWN, SET APART, SENT.` · `AH, AH, AH: I AM A CHILD.` · `I HAVE GIVEN MY WORDS IN THY MOUTH.` · `ALMOND, THE WATCHFUL TREE.` · then, large: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE IN THE BELLY I KNEW THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember you were known first. Settle, and breathe. Notice the things you usually use to explain who you are: your job, your mistakes, your age, what people think of you. Set them down one at a time. Underneath all of them, Jeremiah heard something older: before any of that, I knew thee. If you pray, you can rest in Jeremiah's line: before I formed thee, I knew thee. If you don't, simply let yourself be, for two minutes, without needing to earn it. The bell holds the time.
Before I formed thee. God's first word to Jeremiah: known before he was born, set apart, and sent, even while he said I am a child. Today's word.
Your line: known before the womb. Today, when you feel too young, too old or too small for something, say it once: known first. Day four hundred twenty-one.

pairs: I cannot speak, for I am a child

myth: the text gives Jeremiah's exact age
it doesn't. he calls himself a child, a boy; how old he was, nobody knows.
God touched Jeremiah's mouth
behold, I have given my words in thy mouth.
in Hebrew, almond and watching sound alike
shaqed and shoqed: the almond is the watchful tree.

fork.setup: you're Jeremiah. God has just told you you're a prophet to the nations. you're young and you can't find the words. what do you say?
options: yes, Lord, I'm ready.
ah, ah, ah, Lord God: I cannot speak, for I am a child.
send me when I'm older.
fork.reveal: Jeremiah stammers that he's only a child. God says: say not, I am a child. be not afraid, for I am with thee.

original.note: Hebrew: almond. It sounds like shoqed, watching: God watches over his word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lovely verse for baby announcements.
what it means: a frightened young man is told he was known before birth, set apart and sent, and that God will be with him through the hard years ahead.
what a scholar hears: shaqed, almond, and shoqed, watching, a pun the Latin couldn't keep; and the Catechism cites 1:5 in teaching on the dignity of life.

422.title: The potter (Jeremiah 18)
422.hook: a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand is made again
422.howItsDone: Catholics bring what has gone wrong in their lives to God in the sacrament of penance and in daily prayer, and Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house is among the readings at weekday Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young man named Jeremiah said I'm only a child, and God said before I formed thee in the belly, I knew thee. Your line was known before the womb. Did you remember it once? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Anyone who has tried a pottery class knows the moment. The clay is spinning, it's rising, it actually looks like a bowl, and then one wobble and the whole wall folds over like a tired flower. The instructor doesn't hand you new clay. She says: squash it, wet it, center it again. Jeremiah watched that moment about twenty-six centuries ago. God sent him on an errand with no explanation: go down to the potter's house, and you'll hear my words there. So he went, and stood in a workshop, and watched a craftsman ruin a pot.
screen: `ONE WOBBLE, AND THE BOWL FOLDS.` → `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A PROPHET WATCHES A POT FAIL.`

segments.voice: The scene is Jeremiah chapter eighteen, Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims. The potter is working at his wheel, and the vessel he's shaping goes wrong in his hands. Spoiled. And he doesn't throw the clay out. He gathers it up and makes another vessel from the same lump, as it seemed good to him to make it. Then the word comes, and it's a question first: can't I do with you what this potter does? And then the Douay: "Behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel." Two things are true at once in that workshop. The clay is soft, so it can go wrong. And because it's still soft, it can be made again. There's a word hiding here from yesterday. The Hebrew for potter, yotser, means one who forms. It comes from the same verb as before I formed thee. The God who formed Jeremiah in the womb is the potter still at the wheel. Jeremiah's message wasn't only comfort, though. The next verses are a warning to a whole nation: if a people turns from its evil, God will relent; if it turns from good, the good is taken back. And in the very next chapter Jeremiah buys a finished, fired jar and smashes it in front of the elders. A fired pot can't be reworked. Many Catholics think of this chapter when they bring what has gone wrong to God, in the sacrament of penance, in an evening examen, in a quiet church. The pot that slumped isn't the end of the clay.
screen: `THE VESSEL SPOILED ON THE WHEEL.` · `HE MAKES ANOTHER FROM THE SAME CLAY.` · `YOTSER: THE ONE WHO FORMS.` · `A FIRED JAR CAN'T BE REWORKED.` · then, large: `AS CLAY IS IN THE HAND OF THE POTTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer up something spoiled. Settle, and breathe. Cup your hands in your lap, as if you were holding a lump of wet clay. Now let something that went wrong come to mind. A conversation that collapsed. A habit that slumped. A plan that folded over on the wheel. Don't fix it. Just put it in your hands and look at it. It's still soft. If you pray, you can hold your hands out and give it back to God as it is. If you don't, just notice that it isn't fired yet. The bell holds the time.
The potter. In Jeremiah, the craftsman who doesn't throw away spoiled clay but makes it into another vessel. Today's word.
Your line: made again. Today, go back to one thing that went wrong and give it one more turn of the wheel. Day four hundred twenty-two.

the next verses warn a whole nation: turn from evil and God relents; turn from good and the good is withdrawn.
the Hebrew for potter comes from the verb for forming
yotser, one who forms: the same verb as before I formed thee in chapter one.

fork.setup: you're the potter. the pot on your wheel has just slumped and folded. what do you do?
options: throw the clay away and fetch a new lump.
gather the same clay and make another vessel.
fire it anyway and sell it cheap.
fork.reveal: he makes another vessel from the same clay, as it seemed good to him. then God asks: can't I do with you as this potter does?

original.note: Hebrew: potter, literally one who forms, from the same verb as before I formed thee (Jeremiah 1:5).

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a craftsman, a nice picture.
what it means: a spoiled pot isn't thrown away but made again from the same clay, while it's still soft; and a warning that a fired jar can be broken.
what a scholar hears: yotser, the one who forms, from yatsar, the verb of Genesis 2:7 and Jeremiah 1:5. the potter of chapter 18 is the former of chapter 1.

423.title: A new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
423.hook: a law written on hearts, not stone; the words echo at every Mass
423.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest speaks over the chalice of the blood of the new and eternal covenant, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in the Church's lectionary, including in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the potter's house: a spoiled pot gathered up and shaped again from the same clay. Your line was made again. What did you give one more turn? Day four hundred twenty-three.

Jerusalem is surrounded. The Temple will burn. And in the middle of all that bad news, a prophet is told to write down a promise. It holds a phrase Catholics hear over the chalice at every Mass: the blood of the new and eternal covenant. New. New compared to what? That word didn't start at the Last Supper. It started with Jeremiah, in a city about to fall. Some scholars call these chapters the Book of Consolation.
screen: `A PROMISE IN A FALLING CITY.` → `THE BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT.` → `NEW COMPARED TO WHAT?`

segments.voice: Here's how it opens in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the days shall come, saith the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Juda." Not like the old one, the text says, the covenant made when God took their fathers by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, the one they broke. That covenant was written on stone, two tablets carried down a mountain. This time the writing moves. God says: "I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart." Bowels sounds odd to us, but in older English it meant the innermost part of a person, the gut, where you feel things before you think them. The law won't be outside you, pressing in. It'll be inside you, pressing out. And then: no one will need to teach his neighbor, saying know the Lord, because all of them will know me, from the least to the greatest, and I will forgive their sin and remember it no more. Centuries later, Luke tells us, Jesus took the cup at supper and said, in the Douay: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood." In the Bible, testament and covenant translate the same word: berit in Hebrew, diatheke in Greek, testamentum in Latin. That's where the name New Testament comes from. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's whole passage. Catholics hear it fulfilled in Christ and renewed at every Mass. Jews read it as God's lasting promise to Israel and Judah, and the Catholic Church teaches that God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked.
screen: `NOT LIKE THE COVENANT OF STONE.` · `WRITTEN IN THE INNERMOST PART.` · `ALL SHALL KNOW ME.` · `COVENANT, TESTAMENT: ONE WORD.` · then, large: `I WILL WRITE IT IN THEIR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where the law already is in your heart. Settle, and breathe. Put a hand flat on your chest if you like. Now think of one thing you know is right without anyone telling you. Not a rule you looked up. Something you'd do even if no law said so: telling the truth to a friend, not mocking someone who's down, keeping a promise. Let it sit under your hand. Some readers hear Jeremiah's promise in that kind of writing. If you pray, you can thank God for what's written there, and ask for what's still blank. The bell holds the time.
New covenant. Jeremiah's promise of a bond with God written on the heart, not on stone; the words Jesus took up over the cup at the Last Supper. Today's word.
Your line: written on the heart. Today, when you do the right thing and nobody asked you to, notice it. Jeremiah would call it writing on the heart. Day four hundred twenty-three.

pairs: old English for the innermost part

it comes from Jeremiah 31, long before. Jesus takes it up over the cup.
New Testament means new covenant
testamentum in Latin, diatheke in Greek, berit in Hebrew: the same idea.
the Catholic Church teaches God's covenant with the Jewish people was revoked
the Church teaches it has never been revoked.

fork.setup: you're Jeremiah. the city is about to fall, and the people have broken the covenant God wrote on stone. what does God promise next?

a law written inside them, on the heart.
no law at all from now on.
fork.reveal: "I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart." not a stronger tablet: a different place to write.

original.note: Hebrew: covenant, a binding promise between two parties. Greek diatheke and Latin testamentum translate it.

trapdoor: what you thought: new covenant is a phrase from the Mass.
what it means: Jeremiah's promise, in a falling city, that God's law would be written within people, and sin forgiven and forgotten.
what a scholar hears: berit, diatheke, testamentum: one word in three languages. it's why the second half of the Bible is called the New Testament.

424.title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
424.hook: in the ruins, the mercies of the Lord are not consumed
424.howItsDone: Catholics have sung passages of Lamentations at Tenebrae during Holy Week, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering or Morning Prayer, thanking God before anything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, the law moved from stone to the innermost part of a person. Your line was written on the heart. Where did you catch it showing through? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Here's a strange fact about grief: someone once wrote it out in alphabetical order. The Book of Lamentations is five poems about Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it. The walls are down, the Temple is ash, children are begging for bread in the streets. And four of the five poems are acrostics: each verse, or each set of verses, starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Maybe it was a way to hold sorrow that has no shape. A complete grief, A to Z. And right in the middle of the middle poem, something turns.
screen: `GRIEF IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER.` → `A CITY IN ASHES.` → `IN THE MIDDLE, SOMETHING TURNS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is the longest poem, sixty-six verses, three for each letter. It begins with a man who says, in effect: I am the one who has seen affliction. He's been walled in, weighed down with chains, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken on gravel. He says his hope has perished. Then at verse twenty-one he says: this I call back to mind, and so I have hope. And then the lines today is named for, in the Douay-Rheims: "The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed. They are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." Commiserations is an old word for compassion. In Hebrew it's rachamim, which shares its root with the word for womb, and some readers hear a mother's love in it. Notice what the poet doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is fine. It isn't. The ruins are still there when he looks up. He says the mercies are not used up. Like manna in the desert, they don't keep overnight; they come new, each morning, enough for the day. Tradition gives the book to Jeremiah, though the poems themselves name no author. In the older Holy Week services called Tenebrae, Catholics sang Lamentations in the dark, candles going out one by one. And Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple. Both keep this book for the worst days, because it doesn't pretend. It just finds, in the middle of the alphabet, one thing that hasn't run out.
screen: `I AM THE ONE WHO HAS SEEN AFFLICTION.` · `THIS I CALL TO MIND.` · `RACHAMIM: A MOTHER'S COMPASSION.` · `THE RUINS ARE STILL THERE.` · then, large: `THEY ARE NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan tomorrow's first thank you. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day. Not the whole thing, just look for one mercy that came anyway, in the middle of whatever else was going on. A text from someone. Hot water. A person who was kind on a bad day. Hold it for a moment. Now picture tomorrow morning, the minute you wake, before you reach for your phone. Decide now what you'll do then: say thank you, for one thing, first. If you pray, it can be to God, with this line from Lamentations. The bell holds the time.
New every morning. The poet's line in the ruins of Jerusalem: the Lord's mercies aren't used up, they come fresh each day. Today's word.
Your line: his mercies are new. Tomorrow, first thing, before the phone, thank God, or just say thank you, for one thing. Day four hundred twenty-four.

the ruins are still there. the poet says the mercies are not used up, not that the loss is over.

four of its five poems follow the Hebrew alphabet; chapter three gives three verses to each letter.

tradition gives it to Jeremiah; the poems themselves name no author.

fork.setup: you're the poet. your city is ash and your hope, you say, has perished. what do you write next?
options: that everything is fine after all.
that the mercies of the Lord are not used up; they're new every morning.
nothing. you stop the poem.
fork.reveal: "they are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." the ruins don't go away; the mercies come anyway.

original.note: Hebrew: new (plural), from Lamentations 3:23, new every morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful verse for a coffee mug.
what it means: a line written in the ashes of Jerusalem, at the center of a poem of grief, by someone who still saw the ruins.
what a scholar hears: it sits in the third of five acrostic poems, three verses per letter; rachamim, compassion, shares its root with rechem, womb.

425.title: The dry bones (Ezekiel 37)
425.hook: a valley of bones rattles, joins, and breathes
425.howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones at the Vigil of Pentecost and on a Sunday in Lent, hearing in it the promise of resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem written in the ashes of Jerusalem, and a line that held: his mercies are new, every morning. What did you give thanks for first today? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Ezekiel was a priest, carried off to Babylon with King Joachin, years before the city fell. He lived among the exiles by a river called the Chobar, a long way from home. That's where his visions came, and they were strange. Wheels full of eyes. A scroll he was told to eat. And this one. The hand of the Lord takes hold of him and sets him down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones. Not a few. Very many, the text says. And very dry.
screen: `A PRIEST IN EXILE.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, AND VERY DRY.`

segments.voice: God walks him round about them, so he sees how many there are. Then God asks a question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?" It's a real question, and Ezekiel hands it back: "O Lord God, thou knowest." So God tells him to preach to the bones. Ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. And while he's speaking there's a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin over them. And they lie there. Bodies, but no breath. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, and blow upon these slain, that they may live. And breath comes into them, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The whole chapter turns on one Hebrew word, ruach. It means breath. It means wind. It means spirit. Ezekiel uses it all three ways here, sometimes in the same sentence, and English has to pick one each time. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel. They're the people in exile saying our bones are dried up, our hope is lost. The vision is a promise that a people who thought they were finished would live and go home. Christians also hear in it the resurrection of the dead and the gift of the Spirit. The Church reads it at the Vigil of Pentecost and in Lent. Either way, the bones don't argue their way back to life. They're spoken to, and then breathed into.
screen: `CAN THESE BONES LIVE? THOU KNOWEST.` · `BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.` · `RUACH: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT.` · `OUR HOPE IS LOST, THEY SAID.` · then, large: `COME FROM THE FOUR WINDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring something that feels dead into the valley. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that feels dried out. A friendship that went quiet. A hope you stopped mentioning. A part of your faith, or of yourself, that hasn't moved in a long time. Don't try to make it live. Just ask the question over it, the way God asked Ezekiel: can this live? And give Ezekiel's answer if you can't give another one: thou knowest. Then simply breathe. In Ezekiel's Hebrew, every breath in is ruach, the same word. If you pray, you can pray over it, as it is. The bell holds the time.
The dry bones. Ezekiel's vision of a valley of bones that come together and stand up when the breath of God enters them. Today's word.
Your line: can these bones live. Today, do one small thing for the dry thing you named: one message, one page, one step. Leave the rest to the breath. Day four hundred twenty-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spooky vision, or a children's song about bones.
what it means: a promise to exiles who said our hope is lost: God would raise them up and bring them home.
what a scholar hears: ruach, used for breath, wind and spirit in the same chapter; the bones are joined by the word and given life by the breath.

426.title: I will allure her (Hosea 2)
426.hook: God as a hurt husband who leads his people into the wilderness to speak to her heart
426.howItsDone: Catholics hear Hosea's promise to speak to the heart in the Mass readings, and Catholic retreats sometimes take it up, describing days of silence as being led into the wilderness to listen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezekiel's valley: bone to its bone, and then the breath from the four winds. Your line was can these bones live. What small thing did you do for the dry one? Day four hundred twenty-six.

Hosea's message came to him as a marriage. The book dates him by the kings he lived under, among them Jeroboam of Israel, and it opens with God telling him to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him. Her name was Gomer. They had three children, and God gave each child a name that was a sermon. A son called Jezrahel, after a valley of bloodshed. A daughter called Without mercy. A son called Not my people. Every time he called them in for dinner, he said a prophecy out loud. Hosea's own kitchen table became the picture of a broken covenant.
screen: `A PROPHET HANDED A MARRIAGE.` → `GOMER, AND THREE NAMES.` → `WITHOUT MERCY. NOT MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Chapter two sounds like a divorce court. The husband is God, the wife is the people, and the charge is that she ran after other lovers, the Baals, the local gods, and gave them the credit for her grain and wine and oil. The anger is real, and it goes on for verses. Then comes a word you'd expect to lead into the sentence: therefore. And here's what follows it, in the Douay-Rheims: "Therefore, behold I will allure her, and will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart." Not punish her. Allure her. Win her back. And the wilderness isn't exile; it's where the love story began, when God led the people out of Egypt and they were young. Speak to her heart is a Hebrew phrase for speaking tenderly, the way you talk to someone you've hurt or who has hurt you. Joseph speaks to his brothers' hearts when he forgives them in Genesis. Isaiah is told to speak to the heart of Jerusalem in the comfort chapter we read a week ago. And by the end of the chapter, God promises: I will espouse thee to me for ever, in justice and mercy and faithfulness. The children's names get reversed. Without mercy will be shown mercy. Not my people will hear: thou art my people. Some Catholic writers have read Hosea alongside the Song of Songs, as God's love for his people and for each soul. Some readers today find the husband-and-wife picture hard, with the wife cast as the one at fault and the anger so fierce, and they wrestle with that honestly. Either way, the turn is there in the text: after all of it, therefore, tenderness.
screen: `A CHARGE LIKE A DIVORCE COURT.` · `THEREFORE: I WILL ALLURE HER.` · `SPEAK TO HER HEART: SPEAK TENDERLY.` · `NOT MY PEOPLE BECOMES MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `I WILL SPEAK TO HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let God speak tenderly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the last time you got something wrong, and listen to the voice that started up in your head afterward. Is it a judge? A sigh? A list? Now try the other voice Hosea describes, the one that says therefore and then turns gentle. Picture being led somewhere quiet, away from the noise, and spoken to as someone who is still loved. If you pray, you can simply sit and let God speak to your heart, without rushing to answer. If you don't, try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend. The bell holds the time.
I will allure her. God's words in Hosea, after the anger: a promise to lead his people into the wilderness and win them back with tenderness. Today's word.
Your line: speak to her heart. Today, when you have something hard to say to someone, say it to their heart: gently, and in a quiet place. Day four hundred twenty-six.

myth: after the anger, God plans to lead his people into the wilderness to punish them
to allure her, and speak to her heart. the wilderness is where it began.
Hosea's children were given names that were messages
Jezrahel, Without mercy, and Not my people; the names are reversed by the end of chapter two.
speak to the heart is a Hebrew phrase found elsewhere in the Bible
Joseph speaks to his brothers' hearts, and Isaiah is told to speak to the heart of Jerusalem.

fork.setup: you're the hurt husband in Hosea's story. she ran after other lovers and forgot who loved her. the verse begins: therefore. what comes next?
options: therefore I will shut the door for good.
therefore I will allure her, lead her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart.
therefore I will send her away with nothing.
fork.reveal: the word you'd expect to bring the punishment brings tenderness instead: I will allure her, and speak to her heart.

original.note: Hebrew: heart, the center of thought and will as well as feeling. to speak 'upon the heart' is to speak tenderly.

trapdoor: what you thought: allure sounds like seduction.
what it means: after a long charge of unfaithfulness, God promises to win his people back, leading them to the wilderness where their love began.
what a scholar hears: dibber al-lev, speak upon the heart, the idiom of Genesis 50:21 and Isaiah 40:2; and the children's names Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi reversed.

427.title: Justice like a torrent (Amos 5:21–24)
427.hook: God doesn't want songs without justice for the poor
427.howItsDone: Catholic parishes join worship with works of justice and mercy, and Catholic social teaching, drawing on prophets like Amos, speaks of a preferential option for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea: after all the anger, therefore, tenderness. Your line was speak to her heart. Who did you speak to gently? Day four hundred twenty-seven, the end of the week.

In August 1963, on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, Martin Luther King Jr. reached for the words of a shepherd from the eighth century before Christ. The shepherd's name was Amos. He said himself he wasn't a prophet or a prophet's son; he was a herdsman who tended fig trees, from a small town called Tekoa in the south. God sent him north, to Bethel, the royal shrine of the kingdom of Israel, in a time of money and peace. The festivals were full. The music was magnificent. And Amos stood up in the middle of it with a message nobody wanted.
screen: `1963, THE LINCOLN MEMORIAL.` → `A HERDSMAN FROM TEKOA.` → `FULL FESTIVALS AT BETHEL.`

segments.voice: Amos speaks in God's voice, and it's blunt. I hate your feast days. I won't accept your offerings. Take away the noise of your songs; I won't listen to the music of your harps. That's hard to hear in a church that loves its music. But read the chapters around it. Amos has just described people who sell the poor for a pair of shoes, who trample the heads of the needy into the dust, who take bribes at the town gate where justice was meant to be done. The problem isn't singing. It's singing at the festival and cheating at the market the next morning. Then the line King quoted, in the Douay-Rheims: "judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent." The Hebrew picture is exact. Most streams in that land are wadis: dry gullies that roar after a storm and are empty by summer. Amos asks for something else, a nachal eitan, a stream that never fails. Not justice that flares up when a cause trends and is gone in a month. Justice that runs all year. Catholic social teaching speaks of a preferential option for the poor, and this is one of its roots. Look back at the week the prophets gave us: a boy known before he was formed, a potter remaking clay, a covenant written on the heart, mercies new every morning, bones that breathe, a husband who speaks tenderly, and now a stream that doesn't dry up. Seven pictures of a God who keeps coming back, and wants his people to keep coming back to the poor.
screen: `TAKE AWAY THE NOISE OF YOUR SONGS.` · `THE POOR SOLD FOR A PAIR OF SHOES.` · `NOT A WADI: A STREAM THAT NEVER FAILS.` · `A WEEK OF PROPHETS, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `JUSTICE AS A MIGHTY TORRENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pair one prayer with one just act. Settle, and breathe. Think of a prayer, a hymn or a song of praise you love, one you'd sing without being asked. Let it play in your head for a moment. Now think of one person near you who is being treated unfairly, or is simply poor and overlooked. A coworker, a neighbor, someone on your street. Ask what one concrete thing would let a little justice flow their way this week. A fair word. A shared meal. Paying something on time. Choose it, and tie it to the song. If you pray, you can offer them together. The bell holds the time.
Justice like a torrent. Amos's demand that justice for the poor run like a stream that never dries up, not a song without it. Today's word.
Your line: justice, like a torrent. Today, do the just act you chose, and hum the song while you do it. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

fork.setup: you're at the festival at Bethel. the choir is magnificent. outside the gate, the poor are being sold for a pair of shoes. what does Amos say God wants?

fork.reveal: "judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent." without it, God says, take away the noise of your songs.

original.note: Hebrew: an ever-flowing stream, unlike a wadi that runs after rain and dries in summer.

trapdoor: what you thought: God doesn't like church music.
what it means: worship that ignores the poor is noise; God wants justice that keeps flowing, alongside the songs.
what a scholar hears: nachal eitan, a perennial stream, set against the seasonal wadis of the land; Amos preached at Bethel in the eighth century BC.
